prefill.quotation: This finer level of granularity has the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of urban risk assessments and support decision-making regarding disaster risk management and climate adaptation.
prefill.comment: The authors present building-level resolution as a route to more accurate urban flood risk assessment, but the paper gives no quantitative check against observed flooding: Sect. 4.3.1 only compares the design storm qualitatively with two Hamburg events, and the worked example uses synthetic building data. The accuracy gain is therefore stated as a potential; it can be tested wherever flood impacts have been recorded.

prefill.aida: Building-level pluvial flood risk mapping locates urban flood impacts more accurately than mapping at the scale of sub-city statistical units.

prefill.label: Building-level pluvial flood risk mapping more accurate than sub-city units
Replication in Logroño (Spain) with open data: building-level pluvial flood risk mapping tested against recorded flood impacts
prefill.scope: Whether building-level pluvial flood risk mapping, as proposed in the paper's framework, locates urban flood impacts more accurately than mapping at the scale of sub-city statistical units, when the framework is transferred to another city with open data only. In scope: the municipality of Logroño, Spain (6,315 buildings, 4,617 with residents; its 109 census sections as the sub-city units); the 100-year design storm, with return periods of 2 to 200 years as sensitivity; every index of the framework (social vulnerability, both exposures, both hazard indices, both risk indices and the risk classes) for every building; and, as the reference, the places where recorded storms caused flooding (13 distinct places from local press reports of six storms, 2018-2024). Testable against recorded impacts: the hazard component directly, the risk indices indirectly. Out of scope: validating social vulnerability (impact records do not say who was affected), the paper's own example and sensitivity analysis (reproduced in the Hamburg chain), other hazards, and future climate or adaptation scenarios (planned separately).
prefill.methodology: A Snakemake pipeline (notebooks 01-04), open data only, from download to figures. Inputs: REACHOUT pluvial flood maps for Logroño (SaferRAIN, 2 m, baseline green cover; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.14035876); Spanish Cadastre INSPIRE buildings, building parts, cadastral zoning and addresses; INE Census 2021 indicators and section boundaries; Copernicus Urban Atlas 2018 (water, roads); OpenStreetMap features for reported places without an address. Preparation: flood extents at depth of at least 30, 40, ... 100 cm polygonised on the native grid and reprojected to ETRS89 / UTM 30N, water bodies removed; census population shared among buildings by Cadastre dwellings; ground-floor residents = residents / floors for residential buildings; census proxies for the four vulnerability indicators; street area = gaps between Cadastre urban blocks closed by 25 m, minus water. Risk: building-climate-risk v0.2.0 (10.5281/zenodo.23282971), the implementation that reproduces the authors' Hamburg example, with the paper's settings: TOPSIS with entropy (children 0.3 / elderly people living alone 0.7; welfare 0.5 / education 0.5; 0.5 / 0.5), flood-sensitivity threshold 0.25 x mean and exponent 2, hazard to well-being from a 2 m ring over depths 30-100 cm, hazard to mobility from 5 / 15 / 30 m rings at 30 cm, risk = social vulnerability x exposure x hazard, iterated-mean classes with three iterations. Robustness: alternative welfare proxy (disability pensioners), the sensitivity weights of the paper's text, no ground-floor residents in continuous urban fabric, Urban Atlas roads as street area. Impact test: each reported place, and every other street of the Cadastre address register as the baseline, gets the flooded share (at least 30 cm) of the open ground (not building, not water) within 20 m, the mean hazard to mobility and the highest mobility-risk class of buildings within 50 m; reported places are ranked among the baseline streets and their mean percentile is tested with a one-sided permutation test (10,000 shuffles, fixed seed), for subsets of places, a central-streets baseline and return periods of 2 to 200 years. Scale comparison: the same ranking with census-section values (flooded share of each section's open ground, overlap-weighted over each 20 m zone) instead of street-scale values, tested with a one-sided exact paired sign-flip test on the per-place percentile differences.
prefill.deviation: (1) Hazard model: REACHOUT SaferRAIN (hydrostatic fill-and-spill with Green-Ampt infiltration, no sewer network, 15-min design storm, 26.77 mm for the 100-year storm, 2 m grid in UTM zone 32) instead of the 2-D VISDOM model coupled with SWMM (60-min Euler-II storm of 36 mm, 1 m). Flood depths are not resampled; only the threshold polygons are reprojected. (2) Water bodies are removed from the flood extents: the rain-on-grid model also fills the river bed. (3) Population and social data: census sections shared among buildings by Cadastre dwellings; the paper's example used synthetic building-level data and did not disaggregate. (4) Census proxies for the indicators: children under 16 (not under 10); one-person households scaled by the share over 64 (elderly people living alone); unemployment (welfare recipients); residents without higher education (school leavers without diploma). (5) Ground-floor residents: the open Cadastre has no per-floor use, so residential buildings are assumed residential on the ground floor; buildings with dwellings but another main use get none (the paper's mixed-use rule). (6) Street area: gaps between Cadastre urban blocks, not road polygons. (7) Risk and classes over the buildings with residents; the authors' class rule is kept, so its means include the zero-risk buildings, a case the paper's example did not meet. (8) Method details inferred in the Hamburg reproduction are kept: sensitivity weights 0.3 / 0.7 (Eq. 2 and the authors' results; the text of Sect. 3.1.1 gives 0.7 / 0.3), TOPSIS vector normalisation, entropy in all three TOPSIS steps, three class iterations, rings that exclude every building footprint. (9) Open Python instead of ArcGIS Pro. (10) The comparison with recorded impacts and with census-section scale is an addition: the paper compares its scenario only qualitatively with two Hamburg events (Sect. 4.3.1).

prefill.label: Building-level pluvial flood risk transferred to Logroño with open data: fine-scale modelled flooding locates recorded impacts better than sub-city units; risk indices only weakly (partially supported)
prefill.conclusion:
Partially supported. The paper states that building-level granularity "has the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of urban risk assessments". Transferred to Logroño (Spain) with open data only, the framework's hazard component is accurate where it can be checked: places where recorded storms (2018-2024) caused flooding are among the most flooded places in the open 2 m flood map (REACHOUT), far more than other streets, for every design storm. The finer granularity is what makes the difference: the same flood map summarised per census section (the sub-city statistical units the paper moves away from) locates the same places clearly less well. This supports the claim, including its comparison with sub-city units, for the part of a risk assessment that says where water causes problems.

The claim as a whole, about risk assessments, could only be partly tested. Risk = social vulnerability x exposure x hazard, and recorded impacts (press reports of flooded streets, underpasses, garages, a hospital car park) say where water caused trouble, not who was affected or how vulnerable they were. Social vulnerability was therefore not tested, and exposure only indirectly. The building-level risk indices agree only weakly with the recorded places; this is expected by design (several reported places are roads and underpasses with no residents beside them, where the framework correctly gives high hazard but low risk to residents) and is not evidence against them. The accuracy of the building-level risk classes themselves remains unvalidated.
prefill.evidence:
Test: for each of 13 distinct places reported flooded in local press (6 storms, 2018-2024; 14 reports), the share of open ground within 20 m flooded at least 30 cm in the 100-year design storm, ranked among 512 other Logroño streets (Cadastre address register); one-sided permutation test of the mean percentile, 10,000 shuffles (p = 0.0001 is the smallest attainable).

Hazard (what impacts can test): reported places rank at the 83.8th percentile on average vs all streets (p <= 0.0001) and the 88.6th vs the 143 streets in continuous urban fabric (p <= 0.0001); 12 of 13 places are above the median street, while 57.8 % of streets have no modelled flooding at all. Like-for-like subset (6 places located by Cadastre addresses, as the baseline): 78.3th percentile (p = 0.0064), 82.5th vs central streets (p = 0.0022).

Finer vs coarser granularity: with section-level values (flooded share of each census section's open ground, overlap-weighted over each 20 m zone) the same places rank at the 69.3th percentile vs 83.9th at street scale; 9 of 13 places rank higher at street scale; exact one-sided paired sign-flip test p = 0.010 (central-streets baseline: 88.6th vs 73.0th, 10 of 13, p = 0.0034; like-for-like 6 street places: 78.3th vs 53.1th, 5 of 6, p = 0.031, the smallest attainable being 0.016). Press-only and without-approximate-locations subsets give 82.6th-88.9th percentiles (all p <= 0.0001). Across design storms of 2 to 200 years the mean percentile stays between 83.4th and 89.5th (all p <= 0.0001). Strongest matches: calle Clavijo underpass under the N-111 and calle San Gregorio (99.2th percentile each); the one miss is Paseo del Espolón (no modelled flooding, 28.9th percentile).

Risk (vulnerability x exposure x hazard): mean hazard to mobility of buildings within 50 m ranks at the 63.6th-68.1th percentile (p = 0.028-0.085 across subsets and baselines); the highest mobility-risk class within 50 m at the 60.8th-65.9th (p = 0.018-0.156). Example: the Clavijo underpass (99.2th percentile for flooding) has only no-risk residential buildings within 50 m.

Risk mapping: building-climate-risk v0.2.0 (10.5281/zenodo.23282971; reproduces the authors' Hamburg example, 37/37 classes) on 4,617 residential buildings (150,596 residents); authors' iterated-mean classes: risk to well-being 5 buildings high or very high (1,105 residents), risk to mobility 10 (2,002 residents). Hotspots are stable to the welfare proxy, the sensitivity weights and the street source (70-100 % retained), not to the ground-floor assumption (well-being: 1 of 5 retained, Spearman 0.683).
prefill.limitations:
The scale comparison uses the hazard only: the section-level map stands for a sub-city-unit assessment of where water collects, not for a full sub-city risk assessment combining section hazard with section vulnerability. What could not be tested: (1) social vulnerability - impact reports do not record who was affected; testing it needs impact data on people, e.g. emergency calls or evacuations by address and household (SOS Rioja 112 / Logroño council logs, available only on request and aggregated); (2) exposure, only indirectly; (3) therefore the accuracy of the building-level risk classes, the core output of the framework.

Impact data: 13 distinct places from press reports, a small sample with low power for the risk measures; press attention favours busy central places (a stricter central-streets baseline gives the same result); one place comes from a post embedded in an article, two locations are approximate; several places are roads or an underpass located with OpenStreetMap, while the baseline streets are located by Cadastre addresses (the like-for-like subset of 6 street places still differs from the baseline). Storms are matched to design storms only loosely: REACHOUT storms last 15 min, the reported events 15-60 min with different totals; the result holds for every return period from 2 to 200 years.

Transfer choices that differ from the paper: hazard from REACHOUT SaferRAIN (hydrostatic fill-and-spill with infiltration, no sewer network, 2 m grid in UTM zone 32, 26.77 mm in 15 min for the 100-year storm) instead of the paper's VISDOM-SWMM model (36 mm in 60 min, 1 m); water bodies removed from the flood extents (the rain-on-grid model also fills the Ebro's bed); census-section proxies for the paper's indicators (children under 16 instead of under 10; one-person households x share over 64 for elderly people living alone; unemployment for welfare recipients; no higher education for school leavers without diploma), shared among buildings by Cadastre dwellings; ground-floor residents = residents / floors for residential buildings (no per-floor use in the open Cadastre; the well-being hotspots depend strongly on this); street area = gaps between Cadastre urban blocks. Method details inferred in the Hamburg reproduction (sensitivity weights 0.3 / 0.7, TOPSIS vector normalisation, entropy in all three steps, three class iterations) are kept. The authors' class rule averages over all buildings, including the 85-92 % with zero risk here; their 37-building example did not face this choice.
